---
title: "CLINC150"
---

**CLINC150** is an intent detection dataset with 150 intent classes covering everyday conversational domains (banking, travel, home automation, etc.), with 100 training examples per class. The large number of classes and the short, colloquial nature of utterances make it a natural intermediate step between Amazon and NAF.

Two training regimes were explored: the standard 150-class setup and an extended version that adds an out-of-scope (OOS) class grouping utterances that do not match any of the 150 intents. Both regimes produce similar training behaviour — loss curves and hyperparameter sensitivities are nearly identical, with overall performance slightly lower in the OOS setting. The interesting differences emerge at prediction time and will be covered in a dedicated subsection.

```{python}
#| label: fetch-mlflow-clinc150

from pathlib import Path
import mlflow, os
import pandas as pd

RENAME_COLS = {
    "params.emb_dim":                  "emb_dim",
    "params.n_layers":                 "n_layers",
    "params.n_head":                   "n_head",
    "params.n_heads_label_attention":  "n_heads_label_attn",
    "params.vocab_size":               "vocab_size",
    "params.lr":                       "lr",
    "metrics.num_params":              "num_params",
    "metrics.test_accuracy":           "test_accuracy",
    "metrics.test_f1_macro":           "test_f1_macro",
    "metrics.train_time_s":            "train_time_s",
    "metrics.val_loss":                "min_val_loss",
}
KEY_COLS = ["n_layers", "emb_dim", "vocab_size", "n_head", "n_heads_label_attn", "lr"]

def arch_label(row):
    la = str(row["n_heads_label_attn"]) == "4"
    if row["n_layers"] == 0:
        return "FastText + Label Attention" if la else "FastText"
    suffix = " + Label Attention" if la else ""
    return f"FATE (L={row['n_layers']}){suffix}"

def fetch_runs(experiment_name: str, cache_path: Path) -> pd.DataFrame:
    cache_path.parent.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)
    if cache_path.exists():
        return pd.read_csv(cache_path)
    raw = mlflow.search_runs(experiment_names=[experiment_name], max_results=5000)
    raw = raw[raw["status"] == "FINISHED"].copy()
    raw = raw.rename(columns={k: v for k, v in RENAME_COLS.items() if k in raw.columns})
    for col in ["emb_dim", "n_layers", "vocab_size"]:
        raw[col] = pd.to_numeric(raw[col], errors="coerce").astype("Int64")
    raw["lr"]         = raw["lr"].astype(float)
    raw["num_params"] = pd.to_numeric(raw["num_params"], errors="coerce").astype("Int64")
    raw["architecture"] = raw.apply(arch_label, axis=1)
    raw = raw.sort_values("min_val_loss").drop_duplicates(subset=KEY_COLS, keep="first")
    raw.to_csv(cache_path, index=False)
    return raw

# clinc150 avec OOS (151 classes) — expérience d'origine
df = fetch_runs("clinc150", Path("results/clinc150/runs.csv"))

# clinc150 sans OOS (150 classes) — expérience clinc150_noos
df_noos = fetch_runs("clinc150_noos", Path("results/clinc150/runs_no_oos.csv"))

df = df_noos  # le rapport utilise la version sans OOS

# The target vocab_size=10,000 saturated at the dataset's actual vocabulary,
# producing three near-identical values (8,406 / 8,407 / 8,408) across seeds.
# Collapse them to their average so they form a single dimension.
df["vocab_size"] = df["vocab_size"].replace({8406: 8407, 8408: 8407})
```

## Hyperparameter sweep

This section explores the results across four complementary angles: model capacity and robustness; the effect of vocabulary size and embedding dimension; the effect of the number of attention heads; and training time.

### Capacity & robustness

::: {.panel-tabset}
#### Val loss vs. parameters

A key observation is that **`n_head` and `lr` do not affect `num_params`**. In a standard transformer, the total size of the attention matrices is $4 \times d^2$ regardless of how many heads are used, since $d_{\text{head}} = d / n_{\text{head}}$. Similarly, `lr` is a training hyperparameter with no effect on architecture. As a result, for any fixed combination of `(emb_dim, n_layers, vocab_size)`, FATE architectures have exactly $3 \times 3 = 9$ runs sharing the same `num_params` (3 values of `n_head` × 3 values of `lr`), while FastText has only $3$ runs. This motivates two complementary views:

- **Scatter plot**: all 504 runs, showing the full spread of achievable val_loss for a given parameter budget.
- **Curve plot**: for each `(architecture, emb_dim, vocab_size)` group, take the `min(val_loss)` over `n_head` and `lr`, tracing the performance frontier as model capacity grows.

```{python}
#| label: fig-pareto-clinc150
#| fig-cap: "Validation loss vs. number of parameters"

import plotly.graph_objects as go

COLORS = {
    "FastText":                          "#2196F3",
    "FastText + Label Attention":        "#00BCD4",
    "FATE (L=1)":                        "#FFC107",
    "FATE (L=1) + Label Attention":      "#FF8C00",
    "FATE (L=2)":                        "#CC0000",
    "FATE (L=2) + Label Attention":      "#880E4F",
}

df_curves = (
    df.groupby(["architecture", "emb_dim", "vocab_size", "num_params"], as_index=False)
    ["min_val_loss"].min()
    .sort_values("num_params")
)

ft_archs   = ["FastText", "FastText + Label Attention"]
df_ft      = df[df["architecture"].isin(ft_archs)].groupby(
    ["architecture", "emb_dim", "vocab_size", "lr", "num_params"], as_index=False
)["min_val_loss"].min()
df_scatter = pd.concat([df_ft, df[~df["architecture"].isin(ft_archs)]], ignore_index=True)

fig = go.Figure()

for arch in COLORS:
    fig.add_trace(go.Scatter(
        x=[None], y=[None], mode="markers",
        name=arch, legendgroup=arch, showlegend=True,
        marker=dict(color=COLORS[arch], size=8, opacity=1.0),
    ))

for arch, group in df_scatter.groupby("architecture"):
    fig.add_trace(go.Scatter(
        x=group["num_params"], y=group["min_val_loss"],
        mode="markers", name=arch, legendgroup=arch, showlegend=False,
        marker=dict(color=COLORS.get(arch, "grey"), size=5, opacity=0.3),
        hovertemplate="params=%{x:,}<br>val_loss=%{y:.4f}<extra>" + arch + "</extra>",
    ))

for arch, group in df_curves.groupby("architecture"):
    fig.add_trace(go.Scatter(
        x=group["num_params"], y=group["min_val_loss"],
        mode="lines+markers", name=arch, legendgroup=arch, showlegend=False,
        line=dict(color=COLORS.get(arch, "grey"), width=2), marker=dict(size=5),
        hovertemplate="params=%{x:,}<br>best val_loss=%{y:.4f}<extra>" + arch + "</extra>",
    ))

y_cap = df["min_val_loss"].quantile(0.92)
fig.update_layout(
    xaxis_title="Number of parameters",
    yaxis_title="Validation loss",
    legend_title="Architecture",
    height=450,
    xaxis=dict(tickformat=".2s"),
    yaxis=dict(range=[df["min_val_loss"].min() * 0.98, y_cap]),
)
fig.show()
```

The most striking observation is the **clear split into two performance tiers**, which is much sharper than on Amazon. The lower tier (val loss ≈ 0.3–0.5) contains FastText, FATE (L=1), and FATE (L=2); the upper tier (val loss ≈ 0.7–1.4) contains their Label Attention counterparts. On Amazon, label attention had a small but consistent positive effect — here it **consistently hurts**. A likely explanation: Label Attention must learn one query vector per class — a representation of "what this class looks for in the text". With only 100 examples per class, each query receives too little gradient signal to converge to something meaningful and ends up fitting noise. Mean Pooling is unaffected: it requires no per-class learning at the aggregation step, so all gradient flows directly to the embedding and the linear head. On Amazon (200k examples, 5 classes), the queries have sufficient signal and the class-specific attention mechanism provides a consistent gain.

#### Stability

The violin plot shows the **distribution of validation loss across all runs** for each architecture. A narrow violin indicates robustness to hyperparameter choice; a wide one signals high sensitivity.

```{python}
#| label: fig-violin-clinc150
#| fig-cap: "Distribution of validation loss by architecture"

arch_order = ["FastText", "FastText + Label Attention",
              "FATE (L=1)", "FATE (L=1) + Label Attention",
              "FATE (L=2)", "FATE (L=2) + Label Attention"]
arch_order = [a for a in arch_order if a in df["architecture"].unique()]

fig = go.Figure()
for arch in arch_order:
    color = COLORS.get(arch, "grey")
    vals  = df[df["architecture"] == arch]["min_val_loss"].dropna()
    fig.add_trace(go.Violin(
        y=vals, name=arch,
        side="both",
        fillcolor=color, opacity=0.25,
        line=dict(color=color, width=1.5),
        box_visible=False, meanline_visible=False,
        points=False, showlegend=False, hoverinfo="skip",
    ))
    fig.add_trace(go.Box(
        y=vals, name=arch,
        marker=dict(color=color, size=3, opacity=0.4),
        line=dict(color=color, width=1.5),
        fillcolor="white", boxmean="sd", width=0.12,
        showlegend=False,
        hovertemplate="<b>" + arch + "</b><br>median=%{median:.4f}<br>Q1=%{q1:.4f}<br>Q3=%{q3:.4f}<extra></extra>",
    ))

fig.update_layout(
    template="simple_white",
    yaxis_title="Validation loss",
    yaxis=dict(gridcolor="#e8e8e8"),
    showlegend=False, height=430,
    violingap=0.4, boxgap=0.4,
)
fig.show()
```

The two-tier structure from the previous plot reappears here. The three architectures **without** label attention (FastText, FATE L=1, FATE L=2) all produce tight, low-variance violins centered around 0.38, confirming they are robust to the choice of `lr` and `n_head`. Their label attention counterparts are not only worse on average but dramatically more sensitive: the violins span 0.7 to 1.7+, meaning a poor hyperparameter choice can degrade performance by nearly a factor of four. FATE (L=2) + Label Attention is the least erratic of the three, but still far above the non-LA tier.

:::

### Effect of vocabulary size and embedding dimension

::: {.panel-tabset}
#### Vocabulary size

```{python}
#| label: fig-vocab-clinc150
#| fig-cap: "Effect of vocabulary size on validation loss"

import numpy as np

vocab_vals = sorted(df["vocab_size"].dropna().unique())
emb_vals   = sorted(df["emb_dim"].dropna().unique())

df_vocab_mean = (
    df.groupby(["architecture", "vocab_size"], as_index=False)["min_val_loss"].mean()
    .sort_values("vocab_size")
)

vocab_offsets = {
    "FastText":                          -350,
    "FastText + Label Attention":        -210,
    "FATE (L=1)":                        -70,
    "FATE (L=1) + Label Attention":      +70,
    "FATE (L=2)":                        +210,
    "FATE (L=2) + Label Attention":      +350,
}

fig = go.Figure()
for arch in COLORS:
    fig.add_trace(go.Scatter(
        x=[None], y=[None], mode="markers",
        name=arch, legendgroup=arch, showlegend=True,
        marker=dict(color=COLORS[arch], size=8, opacity=1.0),
    ))
for arch, group in df.groupby("architecture"):
    offset = vocab_offsets.get(arch, 0)
    fig.add_trace(go.Scatter(
        x=group["vocab_size"] + offset, y=group["min_val_loss"],
        mode="markers", name=arch, legendgroup=arch, showlegend=False,
        marker=dict(color=COLORS.get(arch, "grey"), size=5, opacity=0.15),
        hovertemplate="vocab=%{customdata:,}<br>val_loss=%{y:.4f}<extra>" + arch + "</extra>",
        customdata=group["vocab_size"],
    ))
for arch, group in df_vocab_mean.groupby("architecture"):
    offset = vocab_offsets.get(arch, 0)
    fig.add_trace(go.Scatter(
        x=group["vocab_size"] + offset, y=group["min_val_loss"],
        mode="lines+markers", name=arch, legendgroup=arch, showlegend=False,
        line=dict(color=COLORS.get(arch, "grey"), width=2), marker=dict(size=6),
        hovertemplate="vocab=%{customdata:,}<br>mean val_loss=%{y:.4f}<extra>" + arch + "</extra>",
        customdata=group["vocab_size"],
    ))
fig.update_layout(
    xaxis_title="Vocabulary size", yaxis_title="Validation loss",
    xaxis=dict(tickvals=vocab_vals, ticktext=[f"{v:,}" for v in vocab_vals]),
    legend=dict(title=dict(text="Architecture<br><i style='font-size:11px;font-weight:normal'>line = mean</i>")),
    height=430, width=740, margin=dict(l=60, r=20),
)
fig.show()
```

Note: the three nominal vocabulary sizes tested are **2,000**, **5,000**, and **≈8,407**. The last value was obtained by targeting 10,000 tokens, but CLINC150's short conversational utterances do not contain enough distinct surface forms to fill a vocabulary that large. Each run trains its own WordPiece tokenizer independently, and the exact saturation point varies slightly (8,406–8,408) due to non-determinism in the tokenizer training algorithm (tie-breaking of merge pairs, iteration order). Since this variation is an artefact of the tokenizer rather than a meaningful hyperparameter difference, all runs with a 10,000 target are collapsed to their average (8,407) and treated as a single vocabulary size throughout this analysis.

The trends are somewhat counterintuitive: for non-LA architectures, performance **slightly degrades** as vocabulary grows. With only 15,000 training examples, a large vocabulary creates a sparse coverage problem. The embedding layer is a lookup table: gradients are computed only for tokens present in the current batch — absent tokens receive zero gradient. At ~8,400 vocab, many tokens appear only a handful of times in the entire corpus, so their embedding vectors are updated too rarely to converge to anything meaningful. A compact 2,000-token vocabulary avoids this: rare words are decomposed into frequent sub-tokens that accumulate enough gradient signal across batches, and the embedding table as a whole is used far more densely. On Amazon, the 200k examples provide enough coverage to support larger vocabularies; CLINC150's 15k examples cannot.

#### Embedding dimension

```{python}
#| label: fig-emb-clinc150
#| fig-cap: "Effect of embedding dimension on validation loss"

df_emb_mean = (
    df.groupby(["architecture", "emb_dim"], as_index=False)["min_val_loss"].mean()
    .sort_values("emb_dim")
)

emb_offsets = {
    "FastText":                          -22,
    "FastText + Label Attention":        -13,
    "FATE (L=1)":                        -4,
    "FATE (L=1) + Label Attention":      +4,
    "FATE (L=2)":                        +13,
    "FATE (L=2) + Label Attention":      +22,
}

fig = go.Figure()
for arch in COLORS:
    fig.add_trace(go.Scatter(
        x=[None], y=[None], mode="markers",
        name=arch, legendgroup=arch, showlegend=True,
        marker=dict(color=COLORS[arch], size=8, opacity=1.0),
    ))
for arch, group in df.groupby("architecture"):
    offset = emb_offsets.get(arch, 0)
    fig.add_trace(go.Scatter(
        x=group["emb_dim"] + offset, y=group["min_val_loss"],
        mode="markers", name=arch, legendgroup=arch, showlegend=False,
        marker=dict(color=COLORS.get(arch, "grey"), size=5, opacity=0.15),
        hovertemplate="emb_dim=%{customdata}<br>val_loss=%{y:.4f}<extra>" + arch + "</extra>",
        customdata=group["emb_dim"],
    ))
for arch, group in df_emb_mean.groupby("architecture"):
    offset = emb_offsets.get(arch, 0)
    fig.add_trace(go.Scatter(
        x=group["emb_dim"] + offset, y=group["min_val_loss"],
        mode="lines+markers", name=arch, legendgroup=arch, showlegend=False,
        line=dict(color=COLORS.get(arch, "grey"), width=2), marker=dict(size=6),
        hovertemplate="emb_dim=%{customdata}<br>mean val_loss=%{y:.4f}<extra>" + arch + "</extra>",
        customdata=group["emb_dim"],
    ))
fig.update_layout(
    xaxis_title="Embedding dimension", yaxis_title="Validation loss",
    xaxis=dict(tickvals=emb_vals, ticktext=[str(v) for v in emb_vals]),
    legend=dict(title=dict(text="Architecture<br><i style='font-size:11px;font-weight:normal'>line = mean</i>")),
    height=430, width=740, margin=dict(l=60, r=20),
)
fig.show()
```

Embedding dimension has a clear and consistent effect: **all architectures improve as `emb_dim` grows**, with the steepest gains between 64 and 256. Beyond 256, returns diminish but do not vanish — 512 still frequently outperforms 256, meaning the model continues to benefit from a richer representation even at higher capacity. 150 fine-grained intents genuinely require more expressive embeddings than Amazon's 5 sentiment classes. The two performance tiers remain perfectly separated at every `emb_dim` value: no amount of embedding capacity compensates for the overfitting introduced by label attention on this small dataset.

:::

### Effect of number of attention heads

```{python}
#| label: fig-nhead-clinc150
#| fig-cap: "Effect of number of attention heads on validation loss"

df_attn = df[df["n_layers"] > 0].copy()
df_attn["n_head"] = pd.to_numeric(df_attn["n_head"], errors="coerce")
head_vals = sorted(df_attn["n_head"].dropna().unique())

df_head_min = (
    df_attn.groupby(["architecture", "n_head"], as_index=False)["min_val_loss"].mean()
    .sort_values("n_head")
)

head_offsets = {
    "FATE (L=1)":                        -0.16,
    "FATE (L=1) + Label Attention":      -0.06,
    "FATE (L=2)":                        +0.06,
    "FATE (L=2) + Label Attention":      +0.16,
}

fate_archs = [a for a in COLORS if a.startswith("FATE")]
fig = go.Figure()
for arch in fate_archs:
    fig.add_trace(go.Scatter(
        x=[None], y=[None], mode="markers",
        name=arch, legendgroup=arch, showlegend=True,
        marker=dict(color=COLORS[arch], size=8, opacity=1.0),
    ))
for arch, group in df_attn.groupby("architecture"):
    offset = head_offsets.get(arch, 0)
    fig.add_trace(go.Scatter(
        x=group["n_head"] + offset, y=group["min_val_loss"],
        mode="markers", name=arch, legendgroup=arch, showlegend=False,
        marker=dict(color=COLORS.get(arch, "grey"), size=5, opacity=0.15),
        hovertemplate="n_head=%{customdata}<br>val_loss=%{y:.4f}<extra>" + arch + "</extra>",
        customdata=group["n_head"],
    ))
for arch, group in df_head_min.groupby("architecture"):
    offset = head_offsets.get(arch, 0)
    fig.add_trace(go.Scatter(
        x=group["n_head"] + offset, y=group["min_val_loss"],
        mode="lines+markers", name=arch, legendgroup=arch, showlegend=False,
        line=dict(color=COLORS.get(arch, "grey"), width=2), marker=dict(size=6),
        hovertemplate="n_head=%{customdata}<br>mean val_loss=%{y:.4f}<extra>" + arch + "</extra>",
        customdata=group["n_head"],
    ))
fig.update_layout(
    xaxis_title="Number of attention heads", yaxis_title="Validation loss",
    xaxis=dict(tickvals=head_vals, ticktext=[str(int(v)) for v in head_vals]),
    legend=dict(title=dict(text="Architecture<br><i style='font-size:11px;font-weight:normal'>line = mean</i>")),
    height=420,
)
fig.show()
```

The number of attention heads has virtually **no effect** on validation loss — the mean lines are flat across 2, 4, and 8 heads for all four architectures. This is consistent with what was observed on Amazon and confirms the theoretical expectation: since total attention capacity is fixed at $4d^2$ regardless of head count, the head split is a structural choice rather than a capacity one. On CLINC150 specifically, the task may not require the kind of multi-perspective token interactions that more heads are designed to capture — a single or few-headed attention over short utterances is sufficient. Whether heads develop specialised attention patterns despite similar loss values may become apparent in the self-attention matrix analysis.

### Training time

```{python}
#| label: fig-train-time-clinc150
#| fig-cap: "Validation loss vs. training time"

fig = go.Figure()
for arch in COLORS:
    fig.add_trace(go.Scatter(
        x=[None], y=[None], mode="markers",
        name=arch, legendgroup=arch, showlegend=True,
        marker=dict(color=COLORS[arch], size=8, opacity=1.0),
    ))
for arch, group in df.groupby("architecture"):
    fig.add_trace(go.Scatter(
        x=group["train_time_s"], y=group["min_val_loss"],
        mode="markers", name=arch, legendgroup=arch, showlegend=False,
        marker=dict(color=COLORS.get(arch, "grey"), size=6, opacity=0.5),
        hovertemplate="time=%{x:.0f}s<br>val_loss=%{y:.4f}<extra>" + arch + "</extra>",
    ))
fig.update_layout(
    xaxis_title="Training time (s)", yaxis_title="Validation loss",
    legend_title="Architecture", height=430,
    xaxis=dict(type="log", tickvals=[100, 300, 1000, 3000, 7000],
               ticktext=["100", "300", "1k", "3k", "7k"]),
)
fig.show()
```

The plot is dominated by the same two-tier structure seen throughout this analysis. The lower cloud (val loss ≈ 0.35–0.5) groups all three non-LA architectures — FastText, FATE (L=1), and FATE (L=2) — across a wide range of training times (roughly 100s to 7k s). Within this cloud the three architectures are largely interleaved: there is no clean ordering where more compute reliably buys better performance, consistent with the observation that the dominant driver of quality is architecture choice rather than training budget. The upper cloud (val loss ≈ 0.7–1.8) contains exclusively the label attention variants, and they are noticeably shifted **to the left** — they train faster than their non-LA counterparts. This is not an efficiency gain: it is a consequence of early stopping. Because label attention models fail to improve their validation loss, the patience threshold is reached sooner and training terminates early. Less compute is spent, but as a symptom of poor convergence rather than architectural efficiency.

### Interaction: embedding dimension × vocabulary size

```{python}
#| label: fig-heatmap-clinc150
#| fig-cap: "Mean validation loss by embedding dimension and vocabulary size"

from plotly.subplots import make_subplots

arch_order = [a for a in COLORS if a in df["architecture"].unique()]
emb_vals   = sorted(df["emb_dim"].dropna().unique())
vocab_vals  = sorted(df["vocab_size"].dropna().unique())

vmin = df.groupby(["architecture", "emb_dim", "vocab_size"])["min_val_loss"].mean().min()
vmax = df.groupby(["architecture", "emb_dim", "vocab_size"])["min_val_loss"].mean().max()

n_cols_hm = 3
n_rows_hm = (len(arch_order) + n_cols_hm - 1) // n_cols_hm
fig = make_subplots(rows=n_rows_hm, cols=n_cols_hm, subplot_titles=arch_order,
                    horizontal_spacing=0.06, vertical_spacing=0.28)

for idx, arch in enumerate(arch_order):
    row, col = divmod(idx, n_cols_hm)
    pivot = (
        df[df["architecture"] == arch]
        .groupby(["emb_dim", "vocab_size"])["min_val_loss"].mean()
        .unstack("vocab_size")
        .reindex(index=emb_vals, columns=vocab_vals)
    )
    fig.add_trace(go.Heatmap(
        z=pivot.values,
        x=[f"{v:,}" for v in vocab_vals],
        y=[str(v) for v in emb_vals],
        colorscale="Viridis_r",
        zmin=vmin, zmax=vmax,
        text=[[f"{v:.3f}" if not np.isnan(v) else "" for v in row_] for row_ in pivot.values],
        texttemplate="%{text}",
        textfont=dict(color="#555555"),
        showscale=(idx == 0),
        colorbar=dict(title="Mean val loss", orientation="h", x=0.5, xanchor="center",
                      y=-0.18, yanchor="top", len=0.5, thickness=18, title_side="bottom") if idx == 0 else None,
        hovertemplate="vocab=%{x}<br>emb_dim=%{y}<br>val_loss=%{z:.4f}<extra>" + arch + "</extra>",
    ), row=row + 1, col=col + 1)
    fig.update_yaxes(title_text="Embedding dim" if col == 0 else "", row=row + 1, col=col + 1)

for ann in fig.layout.annotations:
    ann.update(font=dict(size=12))
fig.add_annotation(
    text="Vocabulary size", xref="paper", yref="paper",
    x=0.5, y=-0.12, showarrow=False, font=dict(size=15),
)
fig.update_layout(height=290 * n_rows_hm, autosize=True, margin=dict(l=50, r=20, t=40, b=80))
fig.show()
```

The heatmaps consolidate the two previous findings in a single view. **`emb_dim` dominates**: the vertical gradient is strong and consistent across all six panels — going from 64 to 512 cuts val loss by ~0.07 for non-LA architectures and by ~0.15–0.3 for LA ones. **Vocabulary size has a weaker but consistently negative effect**: the horizontal gradient is mild, but every panel shows a slight left-to-right darkening, confirming that 2,000 tokens is the best choice regardless of architecture. The two effects appear largely additive — there is no notable interaction between them. A striking result at the optimum (`emb_dim=512, vocab=2,000`) is that FastText (0.342), FATE (L=1) (0.343), and FATE (L=2) (0.344) are essentially indistinguishable: once the embedding table is large enough and the vocabulary compact, the transformer layers bring no additional gain on this dataset.

## Prediction analysis

This section examines what the models actually predict — where they agree, where they fail, and which classes are structurally hard. For each of the six architectures, predictions are taken from the best-performing run (lowest validation loss). As noted above, the OOS regime produces similar training dynamics; the interesting differences lie at inference time and are covered in the dedicated subsection.

```{python}
#| label: load-predictions-clinc150

import json, urllib.request, os
import numpy as np
from pathlib import Path

PRED_BUCKET = "https://minio.lab.sspcloud.fr/projet-text-classif/predictions"
ARCH_FILES  = {
    "FastText":                     "cl150nooos_fasttext.npz",
    "FastText + Label Attention":   "cl150nooos_fasttext_labatt.npz",
    "FATE (L=1)":                   "cl150nooos_fateL1.npz",
    "FATE (L=1) + Label Attention": "cl150nooos_fateL1_labatt.npz",
    "FATE (L=2)":                   "cl150nooos_fateL2.npz",
    "FATE (L=2) + Label Attention": "cl150nooos_fateL2_labatt.npz",
}

PREDS_DIR = Path("results/clinc150/preds")
if not PREDS_DIR.is_dir():
    PREDS_DIR.mkdir(parents=True)

preds_by_arch = {}
for arch, fname in ARCH_FILES.items():
    cache = PREDS_DIR / fname
    try:
        if not cache.exists():
            urllib.request.urlretrieve(f"{PRED_BUCKET}/{fname}", cache)
        d = np.load(cache, allow_pickle=True)
        preds_by_arch[arch] = {
            "y_test": d["y_test"].astype(int),
            "y_pred": d["y_pred"].astype(int),
            "X_test": d["X_test"],
        }
    except Exception:
        pass

ARCHS_AVAIL = list(preds_by_arch.keys())

with open("assets/clinc150_labels.json") as f:
    LABEL_MAP = {int(k): v for k, v in json.load(f).items()}

IN_SCOPE  = list(range(150))
```

```{python}
#| label: fig-confusion-clinc150
#| fig-cap: "Domain-level confusion matrix (rows = true domain, columns = predicted domain, normalised by row). Classes are aggregated by domain — with 150 intents individual-level display would be unreadable."

from sklearn.metrics import confusion_matrix as sk_cm
from IPython.display import HTML
import json, numpy as np

with open("assets/clinc150_domains.json") as f:
    INTENT_TO_DOMAIN = json.load(f)

DOMAIN_ORDER = [
    "Banking", "Credit Cards", "Kitchen & Dining", "Auto & Commute",
    "Travel", "Utility", "Work", "Meta", "Small Talk", "Home",
]

def intent_domain(label_int):
    intent = LABEL_MAP.get(label_int, "")

    cm = sk_cm(true_domains, pred_domains, labels=DOMAIN_ORDER).astype(float)
    row_sums = cm.sum(axis=1, keepdims=True)
```

#### Top confused pairs

```{python}
#| label: fig-confused-clinc150
#| fig-cap: "Top 25 most confused intent pairs — bubble size proportional to error count"

import pandas as pd

N_PAIRS = 25

def top_confused_pairs(y_true, y_pred, n=N_PAIRS):
    rows = []
    for t, p in zip(y_true, y_pred):
        if t != p:
            rows.append((LABEL_MAP.get(t, str(t)), LABEL_MAP.get(p, str(p))))
    s = pd.Series(rows).value_counts().head(n).reset_index()
    s.columns = ["pair", "count"]
    s[["true_lbl", "pred_lbl"]] = pd.DataFrame(s["pair"].tolist(), index=s.index)
    return s

n_archs = len(ARCHS_AVAIL)
fig = go.Figure()

for i, arch in enumerate(ARCHS_AVAIL):
    d = preds_by_arch[arch]
    df_pairs = top_confused_pairs(d["y_test"], d["y_pred"])
    # Sort true labels by frequency to group related ones
    true_order = df_pairs.groupby("true_lbl")["count"].sum().sort_values(ascending=False).index.tolist()
    pred_order = df_pairs.groupby("pred_lbl")["count"].sum().sort_values(ascending=False).index.tolist()
    fig.add_trace(go.Scatter(
        x=df_pairs["pred_lbl"],
        y=df_pairs["true_lbl"],
        mode="markers",
        marker=dict(
            size=df_pairs["count"] * 4,
            color=COLORS.get(arch, "grey"),
            opacity=0.7,
            line=dict(width=1, color="white"),
            sizemode="area",
        ),
        text=df_pairs["count"],
        hovertemplate="True: <b>%{y}</b><br>Predicted: <b>%{x}</b><br>Count: %{text}<extra></extra>",
        visible=(i == 0),
    ))

buttons = [dict(
    label=arch, method="update",
    args=[{"visible": [j == i for j in range(n_archs)]}],
) for i, arch in enumerate(ARCHS_AVAIL)]

fig.update_layout(
    xaxis=dict(title="Predicted intent", tickangle=-35, automargin=True),
    yaxis=dict(title="True intent", automargin=True),
    height=560,
    margin=dict(l=20, r=20, t=60, b=20),
    updatemenus=[dict(
        type="dropdown", buttons=buttons,
        x=0.5, xanchor="center", y=1.13, yanchor="top",
        showactive=True, bgcolor="#f0f0f0", bordercolor="#ccc",
        font=dict(size=12),
    )],
)
fig.show()
```

The most frequent confusions are mostly structurally related intents: pairs sharing vocabulary or near-duplicate intent definitions like `calendar` / `calendar_update`, `bill_balance` / `bill_due`, or `order` / `order_status`. This kind of confusion is largely intrinsic to the task and unlikely to be resolved by scaling the model.

#### Model agreement

Rather than asking *which* model is wrong, this view asks: when models disagree, is that because some are weaker, or because the utterance itself is ambiguous? For each test example we count how many distinct intent predictions the three models within each group produce, then look at how often the **majority vote** is correct at each agreement level. The analysis is run separately for the non-LA and LA groups.

```{python}
#| label: fig-agreement-clinc150
#| fig-cap: "Model agreement vs. correctness, separated by label-attention group"

from plotly.subplots import make_subplots

y_true = preds_by_arch[ARCHS_AVAIL[0]]["y_test"]

GROUPS = {
    "Without label attention": ["FastText", "FATE (L=1)", "FATE (L=2)"],
    "With label attention":    ["FastText + Label Attention",
                                "FATE (L=1) + Label Attention",
                                "FATE (L=2) + Label Attention"],
}

def agreement_stats(archs):
    mat = np.array([preds_by_arch[a]["y_pred"] for a in archs if a in preds_by_arch])
    n   = mat.shape[1]
    nd  = np.array([len(set(mat[:, i])) for i in range(n)])
    # argmax breaks ties by lowest class index — majority vote is undefined when all 3 disagree
    mp  = np.array([np.bincount(mat[:, i], minlength=150).argmax() for i in range(n)])
    mc  = mp == y_true
    lvls = sorted(np.unique(nd).tolist())
    xlbl = ["All agree"] + [f"{k} distinct" for k in lvls if k > 1]
    shr  = [(nd == k).mean() * 100 for k in lvls]
    acc  = [mc[nd == k].mean() * 100 for k in lvls]
    return xlbl, shr, acc

fig = make_subplots(rows=1, cols=2, subplot_titles=list(GROUPS.keys()),
                    shared_yaxes=True, horizontal_spacing=0.08)

for col, (title, archs) in enumerate(GROUPS.items(), start=1):
    xlbl, shr, acc = agreement_stats(archs)
    fig.add_trace(go.Bar(
        x=xlbl, y=shr, name="% of test set", marker_color="#90A4AE",
        showlegend=(col == 1),
        hovertemplate="%{x}<br>%{y:.1f}% of test set<extra></extra>",
    ), row=1, col=col)
    fig.add_trace(go.Scatter(
        x=xlbl, y=acc, name="Majority-vote accuracy", mode="lines+markers",
        marker=dict(size=10, color="#C62828"), line=dict(width=3, color="#C62828"),
        showlegend=(col == 1),
        hovertemplate="%{x}<br>accuracy: %{y:.1f}%<extra></extra>",
    ), row=1, col=col)

fig.update_yaxes(title_text="%", range=[0, 100], row=1, col=1)
fig.update_layout(
    template="simple_white", height=400,
    legend=dict(orientation="h", x=0.5, xanchor="center", y=-0.18, yanchor="top"),
    margin=dict(t=40, b=80, r=20, l=60),
)
fig.show()
```

Note: when all three models predict different classes ("3 distinct"), there is no true majority. The vote is broken by taking the lowest class index among the three predictions — the accuracy shown in that column should therefore be interpreted with caution.

#### Hardness map

```{python}
#| label: fig-hardness-clinc150
#| fig-cap: "Number of models (out of 6) that correctly classify each class, grouped by domain"

import json

with open("assets/clinc150_domains.json") as f:
    INTENT_TO_DOMAIN = json.load(f)

# Per-class correctness count across all 6 models
correctness = {}
for c in IN_SCOPE:
    correctness[c] = sum(
        int((preds_by_arch[a]["y_pred"][preds_by_arch[a]["y_test"] == c] == c).all()
            if (preds_by_arch[a]["y_test"] == c).sum() == 0
            else (preds_by_arch[a]["y_pred"][preds_by_arch[a]["y_test"] == c] == c).mean() > 0.5)
        for a in ARCHS_AVAIL
    )

# Actually: count models where per-class accuracy > 0.5
n_models = len(ARCHS_AVAIL)
class_scores = {}
for c in IN_SCOPE:
    scores = []
    for a in ARCHS_AVAIL:
        mask = preds_by_arch[a]["y_test"] == c
        if mask.sum() == 0:
            scores.append(0)
        else:
            acc = (preds_by_arch[a]["y_pred"][mask] == c).mean()
            scores.append(acc)
    class_scores[c] = scores

# Group by domain
domain_classes = {}
for c in IN_SCOPE:
    intent = LABEL_MAP.get(c, "")
    dom = INTENT_TO_DOMAIN.get(intent, "Other")
    domain_classes.setdefault(dom, []).append(c)

domain_order_hm = sorted(domain_classes.keys())

rows_z, rows_text, rows_y, rows_x = [], [], [], []
for dom in domain_order_hm:
    classes = sorted(domain_classes[dom], key=lambda c: -np.mean(class_scores[c]))
    for c in classes:
        mean_acc = np.mean(class_scores[c])
        rows_z.append(mean_acc)
        rows_text.append(f"{LABEL_MAP.get(c, str(c))}<br>mean acc: {mean_acc:.2f}")
        rows_y.append(dom)
        rows_x.append(LABEL_MAP.get(c, str(c)))

# Build heatmap: one row per domain, columns = classes within domain (pad to same width)
max_per_dom = max(len(v) for v in domain_classes.values())
z_matrix, text_matrix, x_labels = [], [], []
for dom in domain_order_hm:
    classes = sorted(domain_classes[dom], key=lambda c: -np.mean(class_scores[c]))
    row_z, row_text = [], []
    for c in classes:
        mean_acc = np.mean(class_scores[c])
        row_z.append(mean_acc)
        row_text.append(f"{LABEL_MAP.get(c, str(c))}: {mean_acc:.2f}")
    while len(row_z) < max_per_dom:
        row_z.append(None)
        row_text.append("")
    z_matrix.append(row_z)
    text_matrix.append(row_text)

fig = go.Figure(go.Heatmap(
    z=z_matrix,
    y=domain_order_hm,
    colorscale="RdYlGn",
    zmin=0, zmax=1,
    text=text_matrix,
    hovertemplate="%{text}<extra></extra>",
    showscale=True,
    colorbar=dict(title="Mean accuracy<br>across 6 models", thickness=15),
))
fig.update_layout(
    xaxis=dict(showticklabels=False, title="Classes (sorted by accuracy within domain)"),
    yaxis=dict(title="Domain"),
    height=400,
    margin=dict(l=140, r=20, t=20, b=60),
)
fig.show()
```

Each row is a domain; each cell is one intent class, coloured by its mean per-class accuracy averaged across the six architectures. Green cells are easy classes (all models agree and are correct); red cells are universally hard ones. White/grey gaps simply pad shorter domains to the same width.

### Comparison: with OOS vs. without OOS

This section compares the two training regimes head-to-head: models trained on the full dataset including the out-of-scope class (151 classes) versus models trained without it (150 classes). All comparisons are restricted to **in-scope examples only** so the evaluation target is identical in both cases.

```{python}
#| label: load-oos-preds

OOS_ARCH_FILES = {
    "FastText":                     "cl150_fasttext.npz",
    "FastText + Label Attention":   "cl150_fasttext_labatt.npz",
    "FATE (L=1)":                   "cl150_fateL1.npz",
    "FATE (L=1) + Label Attention": "cl150_fateL1_labatt.npz",
    "FATE (L=2)":                   "cl150_fateL2.npz",
    "FATE (L=2) + Label Attention": "cl150_fateL2_labatt.npz",
}
OOS_LABEL_IDX = 150
IN_SCOPE_150  = list(range(150))

preds_oos = {}
for arch, fname in OOS_ARCH_FILES.items():
    cache = PREDS_DIR / fname
    try:
        if not cache.exists():
            urllib.request.urlretrieve(f"{PRED_BUCKET}/{fname}", cache)
        d = np.load(cache, allow_pickle=True)
        y_test_full = d["y_test"].astype(int)
        y_pred_full = d["y_pred"].astype(int)
        mask = y_test_full != OOS_LABEL_IDX
        preds_oos[arch] = {
            "y_test":      y_test_full[mask],
            "y_pred":      y_pred_full[mask],
            "y_test_full": y_test_full,
            "y_pred_full": y_pred_full,
        }
    except Exception:
        pass
```

```{python}
  window.cmCl150OosChange=function(val){{

    Plotly.restyle("cm-cl150-oos",{{visible:vis}});
  }};
}})();
</script>
"""
HTML(html)
```

Same format as the confusion matrix in the Predictions section, with an extra "OOS" row (true OOS examples) and "OOS" column (examples predicted as OOS). The diagonal entry of the OOS row shows how well the model identifies actual out-of-scope utterances; the OOS column reveals which in-scope domains are most contaminated.

#### Global accuracy

```{python}

#| fig-cap: "Test accuracy on in-scope classes: with OOS training vs. without"
```

#### OOS contamination & accuracy impact

```{python}
#| label: fig-oos-dumbbell
#| fig-cap: "Top 10 most OOS-contaminated classes: per-class accuracy with vs. without OOS training (FATE L=2)"

from sklearn.metrics import confusion_matrix

ref_arch = "FATE (L=2)"
y_test_full = preds_oos[ref_arch]["y_test_full"]
y_pred_full = preds_oos[ref_arch]["y_pred_full"]

contam_class = {}
for c in IN_SCOPE_150:
    mask_c = y_test_full == c
    contam_class[c] = (y_pred_full[mask_c] == OOS_LABEL_IDX).mean() * 100 if mask_c.sum() > 0 else 0.0

def per_class_acc(y_test, y_pred, classes):
    cm = confusion_matrix(y_test, y_pred, labels=classes)
    return {classes[i]: cm[i, i] / cm[i].sum() if cm[i].sum() > 0 else 0.0
            for i in range(len(classes))}

acc_noos = per_class_acc(preds_by_arch[ref_arch]["y_test"],
                         preds_by_arch[ref_arch]["y_pred"], IN_SCOPE)
acc_oos  = per_class_acc(preds_oos[ref_arch]["y_test"],
                         preds_oos[ref_arch]["y_pred"], IN_SCOPE_150)

top10      = sorted(contam_class, key=contam_class.get, reverse=True)[:10]
labels_db  = [LABEL_MAP.get(c, str(c)) for c in top10][::-1]
contam_v   = [contam_class[c] for c in top10][::-1]
acc_noos_v = [acc_noos.get(c, 0) for c in top10][::-1]
acc_oos_v  = [acc_oos.get(c, 0)  for c in top10][::-1]

fig = go.Figure()

for i, label in enumerate(labels_db):
    fig.add_trace(go.Scatter(
        x=[acc_oos_v[i], acc_noos_v[i]], y=[label, label],
        mode="lines", line=dict(color="#bbb", width=2),
        showlegend=False, hoverinfo="skip",
    ))

fig.add_trace(go.Scatter(
    x=acc_oos_v, y=labels_db, mode="markers",
    name="With OOS", marker=dict(color="#FF8C00", size=12),
    hovertemplate="%{y}<br>with OOS: %{x:.2f}<extra></extra>",
))
fig.add_trace(go.Scatter(
    x=acc_noos_v, y=labels_db, mode="markers",
    name="Without OOS", marker=dict(color="#2196F3", size=12),
    hovertemplate="%{y}<br>without OOS: %{x:.2f}<extra></extra>",
))

for i, label in enumerate(labels_db):
    fig.add_annotation(
        x=max(acc_oos_v[i], acc_noos_v[i]) + 0.02,
        y=label, text=f"{contam_v[i]:.0f}% OOS",
        showarrow=False, font=dict(size=10, color="#CC0000"), xanchor="left",
    )

fig.update_layout(
    xaxis=dict(title="Per-class accuracy", range=[0, 1.15]),
    template="simple_white", height=400,
    legend=dict(orientation="h", x=0.5, xanchor="center", y=-0.15, yanchor="top"),
    margin=dict(l=180, r=80, t=20, b=60),
)
fig.show()
```

Each row shows one of the 10 most OOS-contaminated classes. The **orange dot** is the per-class accuracy of the model trained *with* OOS; the **blue dot** is the accuracy of the model trained *without* OOS. The red annotation gives the contamination rate — the share of that class's test examples that the with-OOS model incorrectly predicted as OOS instead of the correct intent.

Two distinct patterns emerge. For classes where the two dots **overlap** (e.g. `book_flight`, `spending_history`, `measurement_conversion`), contamination exists but does not translate into an accuracy drop: even though a fraction of examples get absorbed by the OOS catch-all, the model still classifies the remainder correctly, and the overall per-class accuracy is unaffected. For classes where the **orange dot sits clearly to the left of the blue** (e.g. `distance`, `change_ai_name`), the with-OOS model has systematically learned to treat these intents as out-of-scope, causing a substantial accuracy loss that disappears once the OOS class is removed from training. These are the intents whose surface forms — generic, open-ended queries — overlap most with what a real OOS utterance looks like, making them vulnerable to the OOS attractor.

#### Error migration

```{python}
#| label: fig-oos-migration
#| fig-cap: "Error type for examples the with-OOS model gets wrong but the no-OOS model gets right (FATE L=2)"

ref_arch = "FATE (L=2)"
yt_noos = preds_by_arch[ref_arch]["y_test"]
yp_noos = preds_by_arch[ref_arch]["y_pred"]
yt_oos  = preds_oos[ref_arch]["y_test"]
yp_oos  = preds_oos[ref_arch]["y_pred"]

pred_to_oos, pred_to_other = 0, 0
for idx in range(len(yt_noos)):
    true_c = yt_noos[idx]
    if yp_noos[idx] == true_c and yp_oos[idx] != true_c:
        if yp_oos[idx] == OOS_LABEL_IDX:
            pred_to_oos += 1
        else:
            pred_to_other += 1

total = pred_to_oos + pred_to_other if pred_to_oos + pred_to_other > 0 else 1

fig = go.Figure(go.Bar(
    x=["Absorbed by OOS class", "Confused with another in-scope class"],
    y=[pred_to_oos, pred_to_other],
    marker_color=["#CC0000", "#FF8C00"],
    text=[f"{pred_to_oos}<br>({pred_to_oos/total*100:.0f}%)",
          f"{pred_to_other}<br>({pred_to_other/total*100:.0f}%)"],
    textposition="outside",
    hovertemplate="%{x}<br>count: %{y}<extra></extra>",
))
fig.update_layout(
    yaxis=dict(title="Number of examples", range=[0, max(pred_to_oos, pred_to_other) * 1.25]),
    template="simple_white", height=400,
    margin=dict(t=40, b=60, l=70, r=20),
)
fig.show()
```

This chart isolates examples where **adding OOS training directly causes a mistake** — i.e. the no-OOS model is correct but the with-OOS model is wrong on the same example. Among those cases, it answers: *why* does the with-OOS model fail?

- **Absorbed by OOS class** (red): the model explicitly routes the example to the OOS catch-all. The OOS class acts as a drain that pulls in-scope utterances. This is a *direct* effect of OOS training — the model has learned to treat certain in-scope phrasing as out-of-scope.
- **Confused with another in-scope class** (orange): the OOS class is not the predicted label, but training with it has still shifted the decision boundaries enough to break a classification that was previously correct. This is an *indirect* effect — the in-scope label space has been reorganised by the presence of the OOS attractor during training.

The balance between the two bars tells us whether OOS contamination is primarily a direct routing problem or a more diffuse boundary distortion.

:::

## Explainability

Four complementary instruments are used throughout:

- **Layer Integrated Gradients (Captum)** : a gradient-based, post-hoc attribution method that assigns every input word a *signed* score for every class: positive = pushes the prediction toward that intent, negative = pushes away. It only needs a forward+backward pass through the model, so it can be computed identically for both architectures which is exactly what makes the comparison fair.
- **Label-attention weights** : for the Label Attention model only: the *raw cross-attention weights* between each class query and the utterance's tokens — an explanation built into the architecture, rather than reconstructed after the fact.
- **Self-attention matrices** : both models are built on the same transformer backbone, so we can also peek at how the encoder itself distributes attention across the utterance, layer by layer, before any classification happens.
- **Class direction vectors** : we compare two 150×256 matrices, one per model: the label-attention queries from the Label Attention model, and the weight matrix of the linear classification head from the Mean Pooling model. We examine how the 150 intent class vectors are arranged relative to each other in each matrix, to see what each architecture's internal geometry reveals about the intent space.
- **A faithfulness (word-deletion) stress test** : attribution scores are only useful if they reflect what the model *actually* relies on, so we test this directly: delete the highest-scoring words and watch the predicted probability collapse (or not).

```{python}
#| label: load-explain-artifacts

import os
import tempfile
from pathlib import Path
from collections import defaultdict

os.environ["MLFLOW_ENABLE_ARTIFACTS_PROGRESS_BAR"] = "false"

import mlflow
import numpy as np
import plotly.graph_objects as go
from plotly.subplots import make_subplots

EXPLAIN_RUN_LABATT  = "fb8ab8ee46654d2bbec71c756b6552bc"
EXPLAIN_RUN_POOLING = "1c9439a33bb1470d9aaed4b0fb810e96"

_ARTIFACT_NAMES = ["captum.npz", "label_attn.npz", "class_vectors.npz", "self_attn.npz", "faithfulness.npz"]

def _load_artifact(run_id: str, name: str):
    """Download (and cache) one explainability artifact for run_id; None if unavailable."""
    if not run_id or run_id.startswith("?"):
        return None
    _RUN_LABEL = {EXPLAIN_RUN_LABATT: "labatt", EXPLAIN_RUN_POOLING: "pooling"}
    cache_dir = Path("results/clinc150/explain") / _RUN_LABEL.get(run_id, run_id[:8])
    cache_dir.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)
    cache = cache_dir / name
    sentinel = cache_dir / (name + ".missing")
    if sentinel.exists():
        return None
    if cache.exists():
        return np.load(cache, allow_pickle=True)
    try:
        client = mlflow.MlflowClient()
        with tempfile.TemporaryDirectory() as tmp:
            local = client.download_artifacts(run_id, f"explainability/{name}", dst_path=tmp)
            d = np.load(local, allow_pickle=True)
            np.savez(str(cache), **{k: d[k] for k in d.files})
        return np.load(cache, allow_pickle=True)
    except Exception:
        sentinel.touch()
        return None

cap_la, lat_la, cv_la, sa_la, fai_la = (_load_artifact(EXPLAIN_RUN_LABATT,  n) for n in _ARTIFACT_NAMES)
cap_pl, lat_pl, cv_pl, sa_pl, fai_pl = (_load_artifact(EXPLAIN_RUN_POOLING, n) for n in _ARTIFACT_NAMES)

HAS_LA   = cap_la is not None
HAS_PL   = cap_pl is not None
HAS_BOTH = HAS_LA and HAS_PL

if not HAS_LA:
    print("Explainability artifacts not yet available — re-run src/explain.py")
else:
    N_CLS = cap_la["word_attn"][0].shape[0]
    PALETTE = [f"hsl({int(i * 360 / N_CLS)}, 70%, 50%)" for i in range(N_CLS)]

    if "class_names" in cap_la.files:
        CLASS_NAMES = [str(c) for c in cap_la["class_names"]]
    else:
        import json as _json
        with open("assets/clinc150_labels.json") as _f:
            _lmap = _json.load(_f)
        CLASS_NAMES = [_lmap[str(i)] for i in range(N_CLS)]

    MODEL_LABELS = {"labatt": "Label Attention", "pooling": "Mean Pooling"}
    CAPTUM       = {"labatt": cap_la, "pooling": cap_pl}
    LABEL_ATTN   = {"labatt": lat_la, "pooling": lat_pl}
    CLASS_VECS   = {"labatt": cv_la,  "pooling": cv_pl}
    SELF_ATTN    = {"labatt": sa_la,  "pooling": sa_pl}
    FAITHFUL     = {"labatt": fai_la, "pooling": fai_pl}
    MODEL_KEYS   = [k for k in ("labatt", "pooling") if CAPTUM[k] is not None]

    def _class_sorted(cap, i: int) -> np.ndarray:
        """Reorder word_attn[i]'s rows from confidence rank back to actual class index."""
        inv = np.argsort(cap["class_order"][i])
        return cap["word_attn"][i][inv]
```

### Word attributions

The fastest way to *trust* or distrust an explanation is to look at it on a real utterance. The figure below renders a handful of test utterances as **highlighted text**: each word's background is shaded in proportion to its Captum attribution score. **Green = pushes toward the selected intent, red = pushes away from it**, with colour intensity proportional to `|score| / max|score|` within that utterance. When a model predicts incorrectly, you can toggle between **predicted** and **true** class to compare what the model *thought* it was reading versus what it should have read.

The selection covers four informative cases: utterances where the two architectures **disagree** on the predicted intent; a couple where they **agree and are correct**; cases where **both are wrong**; and cases where **Mean Pooling is correct but Label Attention is not**.

```{python}
#| label: fig-explain-highlight
#| fig-cap: "Highlighted-text view of Captum attributions. When pred ≠ true, toggle between predicted and true class."
import json
from IPython.display import HTML, display

if not HAS_LA:
    out = HTML("<p>Artifacts not yet available.</p>")
else:
    y_true_la = cap_la["y_true"].astype(int)
    y_pred_la = cap_la["y_pred"].astype(int)
    rng = np.random.default_rng(11)

    picks: list = []
    if HAS_BOTH:
        y_pred_pl = cap_pl["y_pred"].astype(int)
        disagree  = np.where(y_pred_la != y_pred_pl)[0]
        rng.shuffle(disagree)
        picks += disagree[:3].tolist()
        agree_ok = np.where((y_pred_la == y_pred_pl) & (y_pred_la == y_true_la))[0]
        rng.shuffle(agree_ok)
        picks += [int(i) for i in agree_ok if i not in picks][:2]
        both_wrong = np.where((y_pred_la != y_true_la) & (y_pred_pl != y_true_la))[0]
        rng.shuffle(both_wrong)
        picks += [int(i) for i in both_wrong if i not in picks][:2]
        pl_right_la_wrong = np.where((y_pred_pl == y_true_la) & (y_pred_la != y_true_la))[0]
        rng.shuffle(pl_right_la_wrong)
        picks += [int(i) for i in pl_right_la_wrong if i not in picks][:2]
    else:
        ok = np.where(y_pred_la == y_true_la)[0]
        rng.shuffle(ok)
        picks = ok[:5].tolist()

    examples_explain = []
    for i in picks:
        i = int(i)
        y_true_i = int(cap_la["y_true"][i])
        words = [str(w) for w in list(cap_la["words"][i])[:40]]
        entry = {
            "y_true": y_true_i,
            "text":   str(cap_la["texts"][i])[:200],
            "models": [],
        }
        for key in MODEL_KEYS:
            cap  = CAPTUM[key]
            pred = int(cap["y_pred"][i])
            mat  = _class_sorted(cap, i)
            nw   = len(words)
            entry["models"].append({
                "name":        MODEL_LABELS[key],
                "pred":        pred,
                "words":       words,
                "pred_scores": mat[pred][:nw].tolist(),
                "true_scores": mat[y_true_i][:nw].tolist() if pred != y_true_i else None,
            })
        examples_explain.append(entry)

    def _spans_html(words, scores):
        amax = max((abs(s) for s in scores), default=1) or 1
        parts = []
        for j, w in enumerate(words):
            s = scores[j] if j < len(scores) else 0
            t = abs(s) / amax
            rgb = "57,255,20" if s >= 0 else "255,30,30"
            alpha = round(0.10 + 0.65 * t, 2)
            parts.append(
                f'<span style="background-color:rgba({rgb},{alpha});'
                f'padding:1px 3px;margin:0 1px;line-height:2.3;">{w}</span>'
            )
        return " ".join(parts)

    cards_html = []
    for ex in examples_explain:
        y_true = ex["y_true"]
        meta = (
            f'<div style="font-size:13px;color:#444;margin-bottom:10px;">'
            f'<b>true intent:</b> <span style="font-weight:700;">{CLASS_NAMES[y_true]}</span>'
            f' &mdash; <i>&ldquo;{ex["text"]}&rdquo;</i></div>'
        )
        models_html = ""
        for m in ex["models"]:
            ok  = m["pred"] == y_true
            bc  = "#2E7D32" if ok else "#B71C1C"
            mark = "✓ correct" if ok else "✗ incorrect"
            models_html += (
                f'<div style="margin:6px 0 12px 0;">'
                f'<div style="font-size:12.5px;color:#555;margin-bottom:4px;">'
                f'<b>{m["name"]}</b> → predicts '
                f'<span style="color:#222;font-weight:700;">{CLASS_NAMES[m["pred"]]}</span> '
                f'<span style="color:{bc};font-size:11px;">({mark})</span>'
                f'</div>'
            )
            models_html += (
                f'<div style="font-size:11px;color:#777;margin-bottom:2px;">predicted class</div>'
                f'<div style="line-height:2.5;">{_spans_html(m["words"], m["pred_scores"])}</div>'
            )
            if m["true_scores"] is not None:
                models_html += (
                    f'<div style="font-size:11px;color:#777;margin:6px 0 2px 0;">true class</div>'
                    f'<div style="line-height:2.5;">{_spans_html(m["words"], m["true_scores"])}</div>'
                )
            models_html += "</div>"
        cards_html.append(
            f'<div style="border:1px solid #e2e2e2;border-radius:8px;padding:14px 16px;'
            f'background:#fcfcfc;">{meta}{models_html}</div>'
        )

    nav_id = "hl-nav-clinc"
    n_cards = len(cards_html)
    hl_html = f"""
<div style="font-family:sans-serif;font-size:14px;">
  <div style="display:flex;align-items:center;gap:12px;justify-content:center;margin-bottom:12px;">
    <button style="padding:6px 18px;background:#f0f0f0;border:1px solid #ccc;border-radius:5px;cursor:pointer;font-size:13px;"
            onclick="hlNavClinc(-1)">← Prev</button>
    <span id="{nav_id}-cnt" style="font-size:12px;color:#999;">1 / {n_cards}</span>
    <button style="padding:6px 18px;background:#f0f0f0;border:1px solid #ccc;border-radius:5px;cursor:pointer;font-size:13px;"
            onclick="hlNavClinc(1)">Next →</button>
  </div>
  <div id="{nav_id}">{cards_html[0] if cards_html else ""}</div>
</div>
<script>
(function() {{
  window._hlCards = {json.dumps(cards_html)};
  window._hlCur   = 0;
  window.hlNavClinc = function(d) {{
    window._hlCur = (window._hlCur + d + window._hlCards.length) % window._hlCards.length;
    document.getElementById('{nav_id}').innerHTML = window._hlCards[window._hlCur];
    document.getElementById('{nav_id}-cnt').textContent = (window._hlCur + 1) + ' / ' + window._hlCards.length;
  }};
}})();
</script>
"""
    out = HTML(hl_html)

display(out)
```

### Corpus-level word importance

Zooming out from individual utterances: which words does each architecture rely on *in general* for each **domain**? Rather than displaying 150 per-class charts, we aggregate the Captum scores across all classes within each of the 10 CLINC150 domains, keeping only words seen at least 3 times. This gives a compact view of the vocabulary each domain relies on — and whether the two architectures agree on what matters.

```{python}
#| label: fig-explain-corpus
#| fig-cap: "Top-12 most positively-attributed words per domain (mean signed Captum IG score averaged across all classes in the domain, words seen ≥ 3 times)."

import json as _json_assets

TOP_K = 12

def _corpus_acc(cap) -> list:
    acc = [defaultdict(list) for _ in range(N_CLS)]
    for i, wds in enumerate(cap["words"]):
        mat = _class_sorted(cap, i)
        for c in range(N_CLS):
            for j, w in enumerate(list(wds)):
                if j < mat.shape[1]:
                    acc[c][w.lower()].append(float(mat[c, j]))
    return acc

def _domain_top(accs_per_cls, k=TOP_K, min_count=3):
    combined = defaultdict(list)
    for a in accs_per_cls:
        for w, v in a.items():
            combined[w].extend(v)
    means = {w: float(np.mean(v)) for w, v in combined.items() if len(v) >= min_count}
    return sorted(means.items(), key=lambda x: -x[1])[:k]

if not HAS_LA:
    print("Artifacts not yet available.")
else:
    accs = {k: _corpus_acc(CAPTUM[k]) for k in MODEL_KEYS}

    with open("assets/clinc150_domains.json") as _f:
        _name2domain = _json_assets.load(_f)
    domain_to_cls = defaultdict(list)
    for i in range(N_CLS):
        domain_to_cls[_name2domain.get(CLASS_NAMES[i], "Unknown")].append(i)
    DOMAINS = sorted(domain_to_cls.keys())
    N_DOM   = len(DOMAINS)
    DOM_PAL = [f"hsl({int(i * 360 / N_DOM)}, 60%, 42%)" for i in range(N_DOM)]

    ROWS, COLS = 2, 5
    fig_corp = make_subplots(
        rows=ROWS, cols=COLS,
        subplot_titles=DOMAINS,
        horizontal_spacing=0.08,
        vertical_spacing=0.20,
    )

    for ki, key in enumerate(MODEL_KEYS):
        for di, domain in enumerate(DOMAINS):
            row = di // COLS + 1
            col = di % COLS + 1
            top    = _domain_top([accs[key][c] for c in domain_to_cls[domain]])[::-1]
            ws     = [w for w, _ in top]
            ss     = [s for _, s in top]
            colors = [DOM_PAL[di] if s >= 0 else "#ef5350" for s in ss]
            fig_corp.add_trace(go.Bar(
                x=ss, y=ws, orientation="h",
                marker=dict(color=colors, line=dict(width=0)),
                width=0.55, opacity=0.88, showlegend=False,
                visible=(ki == 0),
                hovertemplate="<b>%{y}</b><br>Mean IG: %{x:.4f}<extra></extra>",
            ), row=row, col=col)

    for di, domain in enumerate(DOMAINS):
        row, col = di // COLS + 1, di % COLS + 1
        fig_corp.update_xaxes(
            showgrid=True, gridcolor="#f0f0f0", zeroline=True, zerolinecolor="#aaa",
            tickfont=dict(size=9), title_text="Mean IG", title_font=dict(size=9, color="#777"),
            row=row, col=col,
        )
        fig_corp.update_yaxes(tickfont=dict(size=10), showgrid=False, row=row, col=col)

    for i, ann in enumerate(fig_corp.layout.annotations):
        if i < N_DOM:
            ann.font.size = 12
            ann.font.color = DOM_PAL[i]

    layout_extra = {}
    if HAS_BOTH:
        n_tr = N_DOM
        vis  = {key: [j // n_tr == ki for j in range(n_tr * len(MODEL_KEYS))]
                for ki, key in enumerate(MODEL_KEYS)}
        layout_extra = dict(updatemenus=[dict(
            type="buttons", direction="right", active=0,
            buttons=[dict(label=MODEL_LABELS[k], method="restyle",
                          args=[{"visible": vis[k]}]) for k in MODEL_KEYS],
            x=0.5, xanchor="center", y=1.06, yanchor="bottom",
            showactive=True, bgcolor="#f5f5f5", bordercolor="#ddd", borderwidth=1,
            font=dict(size=12, color="#222"), pad=dict(l=8, r=8, t=4, b=4),
        )])

    fig_corp.update_layout(
        height=720,
        margin=dict(t=120 if HAS_BOTH else 70, b=30, l=20, r=20),
        paper_bgcolor="white", plot_bgcolor="white",
        **layout_extra,
    )
    fig_corp.show()
```


### Distinctiveness of per-class explanations

A raw 150×150 correlation matrix is unreadable. A more informative approach is to *select* the most interesting classes according to a precise criterion. Two views are shown below, each answering a different question about the attribution profiles. Use the buttons to switch between the two models.

```{python}
#| label: fig-explain-class-correlation-shared
#| include: false

def _class_corpus_matrix(acc, min_count=3):
    vocab = sorted({w for c in acc for w, v in c.items() if len(v) >= min_count})
    mat = np.zeros((N_CLS, len(vocab)))
    for c in range(N_CLS):
        for j, w in enumerate(vocab):
            v = acc[c].get(w)
            if v and len(v) >= min_count:
                mat[c, j] = float(np.mean(v))
    return mat, vocab

_cls_mats  = {}
_cls_corrs = {}
_cls_domain = {}
if HAS_LA:
    for key in MODEL_KEYS:
        m, _v = _class_corpus_matrix(accs[key])
        _cls_mats[key]  = m
        _cls_corrs[key] = np.corrcoef(m)
    for d in DOMAINS:
        for c in domain_to_cls[d]:
            _cls_domain[c] = d
```

```{python}
#| include: false
_N_SEL = 20

def _full_corr_fig(sel_indices, sel_labels):
    n_keys = len(MODEL_KEYS)
    fig = go.Figure()
    for ki, key in enumerate(MODEL_KEYS):
        sub = _cls_corrs[key][np.ix_(sel_indices, sel_indices)]
        fig.add_trace(go.Heatmap(
            z=sub, x=sel_labels, y=sel_labels,
            zmin=-1, zmax=1, colorscale="RdBu_r",
            colorbar=dict(title="r", len=0.85, y=0.45),
            hovertemplate="x=%{x}<br>y=%{y}<br>r=%{z:.2f}<extra></extra>",
            visible=(ki == 0),
            name=MODEL_LABELS[key],
        ))
    fig.update_layout(
        updatemenus=[dict(
            type="buttons", direction="right",
            x=0.0, xanchor="left", y=1.0, yanchor="bottom",
            pad=dict(b=8),
            buttons=[
                dict(label=MODEL_LABELS[k],
                     method="update",
                     args=[{"visible": [ki2 == ki for ki2 in range(n_keys)]}])
                for ki, k in enumerate(MODEL_KEYS)
            ],
            bgcolor="white", bordercolor="#888", borderwidth=1,
            font=dict(size=12),
        )],
        yaxis=dict(autorange="reversed"),
        xaxis=dict(tickangle=-40, tickfont=dict(size=9), side="bottom"),
        yaxis_tickfont=dict(size=9),
        height=700,
        margin=dict(t=50, b=80, l=10, r=90),
        paper_bgcolor="white", plot_bgcolor="white",
    )
    return fig
```

#### Most-confused intents

We select the **20 intents with the highest error rate** (Label Attention model) and display the 20×20 sub-matrix of their word-attribution profiles. If the model confuses intents A and B, their attribution profiles should look similar (high positive correlation). Hot off-diagonal cells reveal intent pairs that are simultaneously hard to classify *and* hard to distinguish in attribution space.

```{python}
#| label: fig-explain-class-correlation-confused
#| fig-cap: "Pearson correlation between word-attribution profiles for the 20 most-confused intents (error rate shown in parentheses). High off-diagonal values suggest the model assigns similar lexical signatures to different intents."

if not HAS_LA:
    print("Artifacts not yet available.")
else:
    ref_key = MODEL_KEYS[0]
    y_true_ref = CAPTUM[ref_key]["y_true"].astype(int)
    y_pred_ref = CAPTUM[ref_key]["y_pred"].astype(int)
    error_rates = np.array([
        1.0 - (y_pred_ref[y_true_ref == c] == c).mean()
        if (y_true_ref == c).sum() > 0 else 0.0
        for c in range(N_CLS)
    ])
    top_confused = sorted(np.argsort(error_rates)[::-1][:_N_SEL].tolist())
    sel_names_a = [CLASS_NAMES[c] for c in top_confused]
    _full_corr_fig(top_confused, sel_names_a).show()
```

#### Most similar intent pairs

We identify the **20 intents involved in the highest-correlation pairs** (highest off-diagonal r in the Label Attention matrix). These are intents for which the model produces nearly identical explanations despite different semantics — potential blind spots. The sub-matrix reveals their similarity structure.

```{python}
#| label: fig-explain-class-correlation-similar
#| fig-cap: "Pearson correlation between word-attribution profiles for the 20 intents involved in the most similar pairs (highest off-diagonal r). These intents share nearly identical lexical signatures despite being semantically distinct."

if not HAS_LA:
    print("Artifacts not yet available.")
else:
    corr_ref = _cls_corrs[MODEL_KEYS[0]].copy()
    np.fill_diagonal(corr_ref, -np.inf)
    flat_idx = np.argsort(corr_ref.ravel())[::-1]
    seen: set = set()
    for idx in flat_idx:
        i, j = divmod(int(idx), N_CLS)
        seen.add(i); seen.add(j)
        if len(seen) >= _N_SEL:
            break
    top_similar = sorted(list(seen)[:_N_SEL])
    sel_names_c = [CLASS_NAMES[c] for c in top_similar]
    _full_corr_fig(top_similar, sel_names_c).show()
```


### Self-attention and label attention: how each mechanism reads the utterance

Both architectures are built on the **same transformer backbone** : they only differ in how its token-level outputs get turned into a classification decision. For the same short utterance, we extract every layer's **per-head self-attention matrices**, for both models, side by side.

**Reading an attention heatmap**: each cell `(i, j)` shows how much token `i` attends to token `j` when building its contextual representation (rows sum to 1). CLINC150 utterances are short (typically 5–15 words), so the matrices are small and easy to read. A **strong diagonal** indicates local, syntax-like processing; **vertical stripes** (attention sinks) indicate tokens that many others converge onto; a **diffuse matrix** means global mixing across the whole utterance.

```{python}
#| label: fig-explain-selfattn-example
#| fig-cap: "Self-attention matrices per head and per layer, for a sampled utterance. One column per model. Use the ← / → arrows to switch between examples."

import textwrap

HAS_SA       = HAS_LA and all(SELF_ATTN.get(k) is not None for k in MODEL_KEYS)
HAS_PER_HEAD = HAS_SA and all("self_attn_per_head" in SELF_ATTN[k].files for k in MODEL_KEYS)

if not HAS_PER_HEAD:
    print("Per-head self-attention artifacts not yet available.")
else:
    HAS_TOKENS = "tokens" in SELF_ATTN[MODEL_KEYS[0]].files

    n_align  = min(len(SELF_ATTN[k]["texts"]) for k in MODEL_KEYS)
    lengths  = [SELF_ATTN[MODEL_KEYS[0]]["self_attn"][i].shape[-1] for i in range(n_align)]
    mid_idx  = [i for i, L in enumerate(lengths) if 8 <= L <= 18]
    cand_idx = mid_idx[:8] if mid_idx else [int(np.argmax(lengths))]

    # Take the minimum across models: the LA model may store extra label-attention heads
    n_layers_ph = min(SELF_ATTN[k]["self_attn_per_head"][cand_idx[0]].shape[0] for k in MODEL_KEYS)
    n_heads_ph  = min(SELF_ATTN[k]["self_attn_per_head"][cand_idx[0]].shape[1] for k in MODEL_KEYS)
    n_cols = len(MODEL_KEYS)
    n_rows = n_layers_ph * n_heads_ph

    def _tokens_for(idx, L):
        if HAS_TOKENS:
            return list(SELF_ATTN[MODEL_KEYS[0]]["tokens"][idx])[:L]
        raw = str(SELF_ATTN[MODEL_KEYS[0]]["texts"][idx]).split()
        return (raw + [""] * L)[:L]

    def _title_for(idx):
        text   = str(SELF_ATTN[MODEL_KEYS[0]]["texts"][idx])
        y_true = int(SELF_ATTN[MODEL_KEYS[0]]["y_true"][idx])
        bits   = [f"true: <b>{CLASS_NAMES[y_true]}</b>"]
        for key in MODEL_KEYS:
            y_pred = int(SELF_ATTN[key]["y_pred"][idx])
            ok     = y_pred == y_true
            mark   = "✓" if ok else "✗"
            col    = "#2E7D32" if ok else "#B71C1C"
            bits.append(
                f"{MODEL_LABELS[key]} → "
                f"<span style='color:{col};font-weight:700;'>{CLASS_NAMES[y_pred]} {mark}</span>"
            )
        header = f'Per-head self-attention — "{text}"'
        lines  = textwrap.wrap(header, width=70) + [" · ".join(bits)]
        return "<br>".join(lines)

    def _frame_for(idx):
        per_head = {k: SELF_ATTN[k]["self_attn_per_head"][idx] for k in MODEL_KEYS}
        L_ref = per_head[MODEL_KEYS[0]].shape[-1]
        tok_ref = _tokens_for(idx, L_ref)
        z_list, x_list, y_list = [], [], []
        for ri in range(n_rows):
            l, h = divmod(ri, n_heads_ph)
            for key in MODEL_KEYS:
                mat = per_head[key][l, h]
                L_k = mat.shape[-1]
                # If a model has fewer tokens than the reference, strip from the front ([CLS])
                tok_k = tok_ref[L_ref - L_k:] if L_k < L_ref else tok_ref[:L_k]
                z_list.append(mat)
                x_list.append(tok_k)
                y_list.append(tok_k)
        return z_list, x_list, y_list, _title_for(idx)

    vspace = 0.025
    row_h  = (1 - vspace * (n_rows - 1)) / n_rows

    def row_domain(r):
        top = 1 - (r - 1) * (row_h + vspace)
        return top, top - row_h

    fig_ph = make_subplots(
        rows=n_rows, cols=n_cols,
        column_titles=[MODEL_LABELS[k] for k in MODEL_KEYS],
        horizontal_spacing=0.05, vertical_spacing=vspace,
    )

    z0, x0, y0, title0 = _frame_for(cand_idx[0])
    trace_i = 0
    for ri in range(n_rows):
        l, h   = divmod(ri, n_heads_ph)
        row    = ri + 1
        show_x = (row == n_rows)

        for ci, key in enumerate(MODEL_KEYS):
            col  = ci + 1
            idx  = (row - 1) * n_cols + col
            xref = "x" if idx == 1 else f"x{idx}"
            fig_ph.add_trace(go.Heatmap(
                z=z0[trace_i], x=x0[trace_i], y=y0[trace_i],
                coloraxis="coloraxis",
                hovertemplate="key=%{x}<br>query=%{y}<br>weight=%{z:.3f}"
                              + f"<extra>{MODEL_LABELS[key]} L{l + 1} H{h + 1}</extra>",
            ), row=row, col=col)
            trace_i += 1
            fig_ph.update_xaxes(
                tickangle=-90, tickfont=dict(size=9),
                showticklabels=show_x, row=row, col=col,
            )
            fig_ph.update_yaxes(
                autorange="reversed", showticklabels=False,
                scaleanchor=xref, scaleratio=1, row=row, col=col,
            )

        top, bottom = row_domain(row)
        fig_ph.add_annotation(
            xref="paper", yref="paper",
            x=-0.04, y=(top + bottom) / 2,
            text=f"Head {h + 1}", showarrow=False,
            font=dict(size=10), xanchor="right", yanchor="middle",
        )

        if h == n_heads_ph - 1:
            top1, _ = row_domain(ri - n_heads_ph + 2)
            _, bot2 = row_domain(row)
            x_tick, x_bar = -0.10, -0.13
            fig_ph.add_shape(
                type="path",
                path=f"M {x_tick},{top1} L {x_bar},{top1} L {x_bar},{bot2} L {x_tick},{bot2}",
                xref="paper", yref="paper", line=dict(color="black", width=1),
            )
            fig_ph.add_annotation(
                xref="paper", yref="paper",
                x=-0.18, y=(top1 + bot2) / 2,
                text=f"<b>Layer {l + 1}</b>", showarrow=False,
                font=dict(size=11), textangle=-90,
                xanchor="center", yanchor="middle",
            )

    cell_px = 35
    plot_sz = len(x0[0]) * cell_px
    fig_ph.update_layout(
        width=plot_sz * n_cols + 260,
        height=plot_sz * n_rows + 230,
        paper_bgcolor="white", plot_bgcolor="white",
        margin=dict(t=150, b=110, l=160, r=90),
        coloraxis=dict(colorscale="Viridis", cmin=0, colorbar=dict(title="weight", x=1.18, len=0.8)),
        title_text=title0, title_font_size=13,
        title_x=0.5, title_y=0.96, title_yanchor="top",
    )

    frames = []
    for idx in cand_idx:
        z_i, x_i, y_i, title_i = _frame_for(idx)
        frames.append({"z": [zz.tolist() for zz in z_i], "x": x_i, "y": y_i, "title": title_i})

    div_id    = "selfattn-fig"
    plot_html = fig_ph.to_html(full_html=False, include_plotlyjs=False, div_id=div_id)

    nav_html = f"""
<style>
  .sa-nav   {{ display:flex; align-items:center; gap:12px;
               justify-content:center; margin-bottom:8px; }}
  .sa-btn   {{ padding:6px 18px; background:#f0f0f0; border:1px solid #ccc;
               border-radius:5px; cursor:pointer; font-size:13px; }}
  .sa-btn:hover {{ background:#e0e0e0; }}
  .sa-count {{ font-size:12px; color:#999; }}
</style>
<div class="sa-nav">
  <button class="sa-btn" onclick="selfAttnNav(-1)">← Prev</button>
  <span class="sa-count" id="sa-count"></span>
  <button class="sa-btn" onclick="selfAttnNav(1)">Next →</button>
</div>
{plot_html}
<script>
(function() {{
  const FRAMES = {json.dumps(frames)};
  let cur = 0;
  window.selfAttnNav = function(d) {{
    cur = (cur + d + FRAMES.length) % FRAMES.length;
    const f  = FRAMES[cur];
    const gd = document.getElementById("{div_id}");
    Plotly.update(gd, {{z: f.z, x: f.x, y: f.y}}, {{"title.text": f.title}});
    document.getElementById("sa-count").textContent = (cur + 1) + " / " + FRAMES.length;
  }};
  document.getElementById("sa-count").textContent = "1 / " + FRAMES.length;
}})();
</script>
"""
    display(HTML(nav_html))
```

**Label attention heads.** The label-attention module has 4 heads, each producing its own (class × word) attention matrix; these are then averaged into the single aggregated matrix used as the architecture's built-in explanation elsewhere in this section. For one example utterance, the figure below shows all 4 heads' matrices alongside the aggregated matrix. Given that label attention *hurts* on CLINC150, it is worth checking whether the heads have learned anything meaningful or whether their attention is diffuse and unstructured.

```{python}
#| label: fig-explain-labatt-heads
#| fig-cap: "Label-attention weights for one example utterance: each of the 4 heads' (class × word) attention matrix, and the aggregated matrix (mean over heads, bottom row). Use the ← / → arrows to switch between examples."

HAS_LAT = HAS_LA and lat_la is not None

if not HAS_LAT or "head_word_attn" not in lat_la.files:

else:
    try:
        lab_idx_list = [i for i in cand_idx if i < len(lat_la["texts"])]
    except NameError:

    if not lab_idx_list:
        lab_lengths  = [len(w) for w in lat_la["words"]]
        lab_mid_idx  = [i for i, n in enumerate(lab_lengths) if 6 <= n <= 16]
        lab_idx_list = lab_mid_idx[:8] if lab_mid_idx else [int(np.argmin(lab_lengths))]

    n_heads_lah = lat_la["head_word_attn"][lab_idx_list[0]].shape[0]
    n_rows_lah  = n_heads_lah + 1

    def _title_for_lab(idx):
        text   = str(lat_la["texts"][idx])
        y_true = int(cap_la["y_true"][idx])
        y_pred = int(cap_la["y_pred"][idx])
        ok     = y_pred == y_true
        mark   = "✓" if ok else "✗"
        col    = "#2E7D32" if ok else "#B71C1C"
        bits   = (
            f"true: <b>{CLASS_NAMES[y_true]}</b> · Label Attention → "
            f"<span style='color:{col};font-weight:700;'>{CLASS_NAMES[y_pred]} {mark}</span>"
        )
        header = f'Label attention — "{text}"'
        return "<br>".join(textwrap.wrap(header, width=70) + [bits])

    _TOP_K_LAH = 10

    def _frame_for_lab(idx):
        words     = [str(w) for w in lat_la["words"][idx]]
        head_attn = lat_la["head_word_attn"][idx]
        agg_attn  = lat_la["word_attn"][idx]
        y_pred_i  = int(cap_la["y_pred"][idx])
        y_true_i  = int(cap_la["y_true"][idx])
        must      = {y_pred_i, y_true_i}

            ranked = np.argsort(mat.mean(axis=1))[::-1].tolist()

            z_list.append(mat[selected])

            y_list.append([CLASS_NAMES[c] for c in selected])
        return z_list, x_list, y_list, _title_for_lab(idx)

    fig_lah.add_trace(go.Heatmap(

    fig_lah.update_xaxes(showticklabels=True, row=3, col=1)

    fig_lah.update_layout(
```
